evidence: The reviewed views do not vendor sqlglot. The only copy I could read is sqlglot 30.29.0 at /opt/hostedtoolcache/Python/3.11.18/x64/lib/python3.11/site-packages/sqlglot. It is not the pinned 30.31.0, and I did not read 30.31.0. In 30.29.0, tokenizer_core.py defines L_PAREN (line 16), SEMICOLON (34), ALL (245), DISTINCT (289), EXCEPT (296), INTERSECT (330) and UNION (444). tokens.py maps '(' to L_PAREN (130), ';' to SEMICOLON (149), and ALL, DISTINCT, EXCEPT, INTERSECT and UNION to their same-named types (262, 297, 305, 332, 412). A grep of dialects/postgres.py, mysql.py, sqlite.py and dialect.py found no override of those keywords or symbols. So the claim holds for 30.29.0 in the postgres, mysql, sqlite and default dialects. I did not run the tokenizer, and I did not confirm the pinned 30.31.0 source. The verdict is INCONCLUSIVE because the pinned version is unread. To settle it, read sqlglot 30.31.0's tokenizer_core.py and tokens.py, or tokenize the sample statements under 30.31.0.

The claim concerns sqlglot's own tokenizer (Tokenizer.KEYWORDS['TABLE'], quoted-identifier handling, dialect overrides, versions 30.22-30.31). The sqlglot source (sqlglot/tokens.py) is not in the supplied views and a search of the available filesystem found no installed copy. I read readonly.py:61-96, which relies on the property (token_type is TokenType.TABLE at line 91), but that only shows the assumption, not that it holds. Not run: inspecting sqlglot tokens.py across versions, or tokenizing 'TABLE t' and '"table"' per dialect.

Read sqlglot's dialects/dialect.py in the runner's installed copy (/opt/hostedtoolcache/Python/3.11.18/x64/lib/python3.11/site-packages/sqlglot), not a pinned copy of the project's own sqlglot version. get_or_raise (line 1047) returns cls() for a falsy value, so None is accepted. An unknown string name goes through cls.get, which returns None, and then suggest_closest_match_and_fail, which raises ValueError (helper.py:65). Malformed format and non-string types also raise ValueError (lines 1089 and 1103). Dialect.tokenize (line 1286) delegates to the tokenizer. tokenizer_core.py raises TokenError at lines 700, 1132, 1388 and 1399 (e.g. 'Missing {delimiter}'), and errors.py:74 defines TokenError. readonly.py:77-88 uses it this way: it catches ValueError from get_or_raise, falls back to get_or_raise(None), and catches TokenError from tokenize. I did not trace unterminated comments to a specific raise line, and I did not check exotic comma-suffixed settings strings.

readonly.py:48-58 limits predecessors to SEMICOLON, L_PAREN, UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, ALL, DISTINCT (loop at 89-95). The docstring (61-76) says it returns True if sql holds a `TABLE t` query in any statement or subquery, and the claim reads the predecessor list as complete. It is not. PostgreSQL grammar: select_no_parens is with_clause select_clause, and select_clause includes simple_select, which includes `TABLE relation_expr`. So `WITH x AS (SELECT 1) TABLE users` is valid PostgreSQL. Its TABLE token follows R_PAREN, which is not in the set, so uses_table_shorthand returns False. The same applies to other positions such as `EXPLAIN TABLE t`, `CREATE TABLE a AS TABLE t` and `INSERT INTO a TABLE t`, where TABLE follows a non-listed token. The docstring's `exactly when` list therefore omits real positions. I did not check whether a downstream parse still rejects these inputs.

Grep of head view src shows exactly two non-test callers of uses_table_shorthand. (1) rls.py:228 apply_rls calls it, then sqlglot.parse at rls.py:234-237 wraps ParseError and TokenError into RlsError, so a TokenError (same tokenizer) fails closed. (2) whole_row.py:119-125 _whole_row_reference calls _parse_statements first (readonly.py:625-639, which converts ParseError/TokenError to UnsafeSqlError), so any tokenize failure raises before uses_table_shorthand is reached. The only transform before the parse is _mysql_parse_sql (readonly.py:565-622), which raises on ambiguity or replaces only carriage returns inside comment text with spaces, so it does not make a raw-tokenizer failure parse cleanly. Order differs between callers (parse before the call in whole_row, after it in rls), but in both the parse happens and fails closed, so 'every caller then parses' holds in effect. Hostile input tried: an unterminated string such as "TABLE users WHERE x = 'unterminated". The tokenizer returns False and both callers' parses raise.

readonly.py:625 _parse_statements is annotated -> list[exp.Expression | None] and returns sqlglot.parse(...) (line 638), which is a list, so it is re-iterable. whole_row.py:121-126 iterates it twice (any(...) at 122, for loop at 126) safely.

Head whole_row.py:119-130 now parses, raises on any None statement (empty parse tree), then runs the tokenizer-based uses_table_shorthand, then the star walk. Base looped per statement and checked TABLE before the None check on each statement. So the order is not strictly preserved: an input with a TABLE statement before an empty statement previously gave WholeRowSelectError and now gives UnsafeSqlError('empty parse tree'). Both refuse, and no doc I read states this precedence. read-only-safety.md:231 only says unparseable SQL and empty statements raise UnsafeSqlError. For the claim's example `TABLE public.users`, the PR removed it from the unparseable test list (diff hunk in tests/unit/test_safety_whole_row.py), and the doc at line 224 no longer says TABLE s.t is unparseable. That implies it now parses under sqlglot 30.31 and is refused as TABLE (WholeRowSelectError), where base refused it as unparseable (UnsafeSqlError). That would change the message, contradicting 'preserves messages'. I could not run sqlglot 30.31 to confirm how it parses `TABLE public.users` or whether sqlglot yields None statements for inputs such as `TABLE x;;`. So I cannot settle the claim, and I did not run that sqlglot check.

Docstring (whole_row.py:37-42) matches the code path: _whole_row_reference (whole_row.py:119-130) calls uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) after _parse_statements, and returns 'TABLE'; a parse failure raises UnsafeSqlError via _parse_statements (readonly.py:639-640), i.e. 'refused as unparseable SQL'. But uses_table_shorthand (readonly.py:61-96) only fires when TABLE follows start, ';', '(', UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, ALL or DISTINCT (readonly.py:48-58). The claim's wording 'any statement or subquery' is absolute. A candidate counterexample is PostgreSQL's valid `WITH c AS (SELECT 1) TABLE users`: TABLE follows R_PAREN, so the tokenizer check returns False; refusal then depends on how sqlglot parses it (probably a star from 30.30, but possibly a column/table named TABLE in the supported range >=30.22, pyproject.toml:46). Likewise `CREATE VIEW v AS TABLE t`. No test covers these (tests/unit/test_safety_whole_row.py:200-205). I could not run sqlglot (30.22 vs 30.31) to settle whether those parse into a star, so I could not confirm or exclude the counterexample. Missing: running assert_no_whole_row_select on `WITH c AS (SELECT 1) TABLE users` with sqlglot 30.22 and 30.31 (postgres and mysql dialects).

rls.py:228-232 raises RlsError whenever uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) is True, before parsing; that part of the claim is correct. The claim's second half is that no legitimate SELECT is wrongly blocked. uses_table_shorthand (readonly.py:61-96) flags any TokenType.TABLE token that is first or follows ; ( UNION INTERSECT EXCEPT ALL DISTINCT. It is purely positional and does not check what follows. The tests in test_safety_table_shorthand.py:40-53 only cover quoted "table", string literals, comments and the empty string as negatives. So a dialect that allows an unquoted column named table (for example BigQuery, with COUNT(DISTINCT table) or WHERE (table = 1)) could be blocked if its tokenizer emits TokenType.TABLE for that word. I could not confirm that. It depends on the installed sqlglot tokenizer, and I did not run resolved.tokenize on such SQL. Not settled either way.

rls.py:229-231 raises 'row-level security can only scope SELECT-shaped reads; refusing a TABLE statement'. Grep over the head view for SELECT-shaped|could not prove|can only scope|refusing a finds: tests/unit/test_safety_rls.py:371,384 match 'refusing a TABLE statement' (matches new text); test_safety_rls.py:358 matches 'could not prove' for 'SELECT * FROM (orders) o', which raises at rls.py:334 ('could not prove row-level-security scoping...'), unaffected by the new message; rls.py:254 shares the SELECT-shaped prefix; docs row-level-security.md:31 and test_system_prompt.py:85 mention SELECT-shaped only as prose, not matching on the error. No source code consumer string-matches the message.

I could not read sqlglot's mysql.py because the views do not include it, so this rests on the repo code and holds under either tokenization of `--`. uses_table_shorthand (src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:61-96) flags a TABLE token only when it is first or follows one of SEMICOLON, L_PAREN, UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, ALL or DISTINCT (lines 48-58). For `SELECT id FROM t -- TABLE users` (tests/unit/test_safety_table_shorthand.py:48), there are two cases. If the dialect tokenizes `-- ` as a comment, which `--` followed by a space is in every dialect, no TABLE token is produced. If a MySQL version treated it differently and emitted DASH tokens, the TABLE token would follow DASH, which is not a predecessor, and the preceding tokens SELECT id FROM t contain no TABLE token. Either way the result is False. For `''` (line 49), the tokenizer yields no tokens, so the loop never runs and the result is False. The assertion therefore holds for postgres, mysql, sqlite and None, whatever the sqlglot version's MySQL comment handling.

The test is at tests/unit/test_safety_table_shorthand.py:58 (asserts not uses_table_shorthand("TABLE users WHERE x = 'unterminated", "postgres")). The implementation at src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:85-88 catches sqlglot.errors.TokenError and returns False, and other tests (test_safety.py:143-147) assume 'SELECT 'unterminated' raises a tokenizer failure. But sqlglot's source (tokens.py at 30.31.0) is not in the view, and no lock file entry for sqlglot was found, so I could not read what the tokenizer raises or confirm the locked version. Missing evidence: sqlglot/tokens.py and the locked version; I did not run the test.

Doc paragraph (read-only-safety.md:225) matches readonly.py:48-96. Predecessors in _TABLE_SHORTHAND_PREDECESSORS are exactly SEMICOLON, L_PAREN, UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, ALL, DISTINCT; start of SQL is covered by previous is None (line 92). Only a TokenType.TABLE token matches, so a quoted "table" (identifier token) is exempt. TokenError returns False (87-88) and the docstring says the caller's parse then fails closed, matching 'left to the parse'. Absolute-claim input traced: `SELECT 1 UNION ALL TABLE t` has TABLE after ALL, so it is flagged; `"table"` yields no TABLE token, so it is not flagged.

rls.py apply_rls: uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) at line 228 raises RlsError before sqlglot.parse at line 235 (version-independent, no version branch); the exp.Table .name/.alias check at lines 317-337 remains as a backstop (comment at 318-321). Matches doc line 30. Absolute-claim input: `SELECT * FROM (TABLE orders) sub` is rejected at 228 before parse; only returns early if no rules (line 220), which is outside the doc's scope.

Verified: pyproject.toml:46 bounds sqlglot>=30.22,<31, and requirements.txt:104 pins sqlglot==30.31.0, which is inside that range. The diff removes only the `--constraints sqlglot<30.30` recipe lines and changes only that one pin (diff.patch requirements.txt hunks). requirements.txt is compiled with --no-annotate, and no other line in requirements.txt, pyproject.toml or the view mentions sqlglot, so nothing visible constrains it. Not settled: whether every other locked package's metadata (which I cannot read) allows sqlglot 30.31.0, and whether the full closure resolves. That needs running `uv pip compile pyproject.toml --universal --python-version 3.11 --upgrade` or `uv pip install --dry-run -r requirements.txt`, which I did not run. Also not checked: that 30.31.0 exists on the index.

I read the diff and src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py (uses_table_shorthand), rls.py and whole_row.py. Both guards now call uses_table_shorthand before relying on the parse. It flags a TABLE token only at the start of the SQL or after ; ( UNION INTERSECT EXCEPT ALL DISTINCT (_TABLE_SHORTHAND_PREDECESSORS). The changelog says 'every supported sqlglot version', which is an absolute claim. A candidate input outside that predecessor set is `WITH x AS (SELECT 1) TABLE orders`. PostgreSQL's grammar allows TABLE after a WITH clause, so the TABLE token follows R_PAREN, which is not a predecessor, and the tokenizer check would not flag it. The result then depends on how sqlglot 30.29 and 30.31 parse that form, and I could not run either version, so I could not settle that. The 'previously rewrote with row scope on 30.30+' half is consistent with the removed requirements.txt constraint `sqlglot<30.30` (#369) and the new docs, but I did not run it. The pin to sqlglot==30.31.0 in requirements.txt is in the diff. I did not check that CI installs requirements.txt.
